extracted.intended_audience: legislators, constitutional designers, and students of political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and design constitutions and government structures (mixed/composed governments) that balance monarchy, aristocracy, and popular representation to secure liberty and durability. Focuses on institutional devices (bicameralism, executive, checks) informed by human nature and historical patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human nature and limits on power
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are liable to passions and weaknesses (ambition, love of praise, love of gold) that increase with indulgence; these tendencies make humans unfit to be trusted with unlimited power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that because passions 'increase by exercise' and can become 'usurping, domineering, cruel tyrants' or 'a species of delirium', constitutional design must assume imperfect human character and build restraints accordingly. Example/anti-pattern: trusting a single body or person with unlimited authority ignores these facts and invites tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating all authority in a single assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: A single assembly will quickly become an aristocracy, then an oligarchy, then possibly divide into parties and lead to civil war or a victorious general ruling by force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages warn that 'a single assembly will, upon the first day of its existence, be an aristocracy; in a few days, or years at least, an oligarchy' and that factional division will produce armies and a dictator. Institutional implication: do not vest all legislative and sovereign power in one representative body; design safeguards against consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power as a check to power (checks and balances)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent abuse, power must be arranged so that one element of government is a check on another; 'power should be a check to power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Montesquieu: 'power should be a check to power.' The recommendation is to constitutionally distribute authority among branches (legislative, executive, aristocratic councils) so that each restrains the others. Example: separating executive authority from legislative assemblies so neither can monopolize control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral division: separate ‘dividing’ and ‘choosing’ functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative business should be divided between bodies that 'divide' (debate/separate/weigh reasons) and those that 'choose' (resolve/accept proposals), modeled on Harrington's 'divide-and-choose' (the cake) example and the two houses (representatives and senate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harrington's illustration—one party divides, the other chooses—shows a procedural device that induces fair outcomes. The text endorses a two-house legislature (house of representatives and senate) so that debate/proposal (division) and selection (choice) are exercised by different bodies, preventing capture and unfair appropriation of benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as deliberative counsellors, not sole lawgivers
rubrics_metrics.description: The senate's proper role is to debate and give advice; its decrees are 'fenatus consulta' and are not laws until proposed to and enacted by the people or their representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that 'the office of the senate is not to be commanders, but counsellors of the people' and that maturely framed proposals by the senate should be proposed to the people. Institutional implication: design upper houses as deliberative/refining bodies rather than as bodies with unchecked legislative enactment power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harness elite wisdom while bounding elite power
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'natural aristocracy' of wise, wealthy, or born leaders whose counsel is valuable, but their ambition and avarice must be restrained by institutional arrangements so they cannot dominate executive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prescription is to arrange elites together in a senate to obtain their wisdom 'without fear of their passions' by prohibiting them from holding executive authority and subjecting them to controls from representatives and the executive. Anti-pattern: admitting elites into a single popular assembly where they can dominate elections and national direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate executive (governor) as an essential branch
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent executive (the governor) is a necessary branch to check aristocracy and support the representative assembly and senate in maintaining public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text indicates the propriety and necessity of an executive 'the other branch, the governor' to form a threefold structure (prince, lords, commons) that checks one another. Institutional implication: include an executive distinct from the legislature to provide an additional counterweight and enforcement mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed or composed constitution for stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution combining elements of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy (prince, lords, commons) is more firm and durable than pure forms because each estate checks the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises mixed governments (citing Lycurgus/Sparta) for long endurance and suggests that blending the three estates yields the 'highest degree of perfection' attainable. Example: Sparta's mixed constitution lasting 800 years versus Athens' fragile pure democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure forms because of inevitable degeneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure monarchy, aristocracy, or democracy are infirm: monarchy degenerates to tyranny, aristocracy to oligarchy, democracy to licentious anarchy; governments tend to rotate through these degenerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Machiavelli and historical narrative, the text argues that pure forms are short-lived and prone to corruption; therefore designers should avoid constitutions that are purely one form and instead mix elements to prevent the cycle of degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should guard against what men may do (legal pessimism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are intended not to trust what men will do, but to guard against what they may do—design must assume potential abuse and provide legal constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting 'Laws are intended, not to trust to what men will do, but to guard against what they may do,' the guidance is to draft institutions and statutes anticipating worst-case human behavior; rely on structural restraints rather than moral appeals alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure representatives reflect the whole people's interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative bodies should be constituted so they cannot contract any interest other than that of the whole people; representatives should be equal and constituted to prevent particular interests capturing lawmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text proposes selecting representatives 'equal, and so constituted as it can never contrail any other interest than that of the whole people.' Institutional mechanisms include balanced representation, bicameral checks, and procedural separation of proposal and resolution to align decisions with common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect independence of individual members and electoral integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Design must prevent elite factions from destroying an independent member's popularity or controlling elections; independence of members is essential to check consolidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that elites will use 'artifices' to 'destroy his popularity among his constituents, and bring in a disciple of their own place.' Therefore, institutional safeguards (electoral protections, tenure safeguards, anti-corruption measures) are necessary to preserve independent legislators and prevent aristocratic consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure permanence of laws against factional pendulum
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions should prevent laws from becoming the plaything of contending factions such that laws oscillate like the 'vibrations of a pendulum' between opposing groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes a danger where, if factions alternate control, laws cease to be permanent protections for life, liberty, and property. Institutional implication: build mechanisms (bicameral review, supermajority thresholds, constitutional entrenchment) to stabilize legislation across partisan swings.
